audience: Adult who knows Earth's orbit and seasons
prior: Likely assumes winter means farther from the Sun.
objective: Explain both changes caused by tilt.
takeaway: Tilt changes daylight duration and the angle of the noon sun.
editorial_direction: Open on two very different days in Minneapolis.
misconceptions: The axis turns around between the two solstices

chapters.question: What stays the same on opposite sides of this orbit?
chapter_claims: Same planet and direction of tilted axis. Use Minneapolis near 45° north.
stages: Show June and December positions around one Sun.

orbit: The North Pole points the same way in space in June and December. Minneapolis rotates with Earth.
axis: Earth's north axis leans toward the Sun in June and away in December. The axis does not reverse.

chapters.question: Does the city spend the same time in sunlight?
chapter_claims: June daylight lasts longer at this northern latitude; December shorter. Bars are illustrative, not timed observations.
stages: Show tilt before using a one-rotation timeline.
Compare each lit share of a full rotation.

axis: Earth's axis tilts the Northern Hemisphere toward the Sun in June. A city moves through the lit and dark sides as Earth spins.
day: Each bar is one day, not a piece of the yearly orbit. At 45° north the June daylight bar is longer than December's.

chapters.question: Does the same Sun strike the ground in the same way?
chapter_claims: Noon angles at idealized 45° north: 68.5° June, 21.5° December. More oblique rays spread light over a larger patch.
stages: Link daylight hours to the separate angle effect.
Compare both noon angles on the same ground.

day: The two bars compare time in daylight only. Ask whether the same surface also receives sunlight at different angles.
angle: At idealized 45° north, noon sunlight is 68.5° in June and 21.5° in December. The same beam covers more ground at a shallower angle, so less energy reaches each square meter.

chapters.question: What happens across the equator?
chapter_claims: Seasonal pattern reverses at 45° south; both hemispheres share Earth's distance from the Sun at a given moment.

angle: The 45° north noon angle is higher in June and lower in December.
south: Compare north and south on the same June day: it is summer in the north and winter in the south at the same Earth–Sun distance. In December the pattern reverses.

transfer.question: At the same June solstice, what changes at 45 degrees south?
transfer.answer: Days are shorter and the noon sun lower there; December reverses the pattern.
